problems.memo_sentence: The quantum-walk option-pricing model produces option prices that agree quite closely with those from a classical random walk, while its coupling to a supply–demand model generates implied volatility surfaces and transaction-volume patterns that qualitatively resemble empirical option-market data, including higher volume near at-the-money and inverse square-root time dependence in implied volatility.
problems.source_evidence: “The resulting option price model agrees quite closely with the classical random walk model, but when coupled with a model of supply and demand, helps to explain some observed anomalies.” ... “The resulting surface resembles the implied volatility surfaces obtained from empirical analysis of option price data ...” ... “Again, this agrees with the empirical observation that volume is highest for at-the-money options.” ... “The quantum walk model may also help to explain the empirically noted property that the implied volatility includes a time-dependent term that varies inversely with the square root of the time to expiry.”
problems.explanation: The memo presents the empirical resemblance and inverse-square-root behavior as established outputs of the model, but the paper is more cautious: it says the model may help explain these features and that the surface merely resembles empirical surfaces. The wording overstates the strength of the claim.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper shows analytically and numerically that the quantum walk’s variance grows quadratically with time, depends on the initial state in a momentum-like way that can induce skew, and that decoherence can bring the resulting distribution arbitrarily close to the classical case; decoherence is also proposed as a proxy for information, leading to higher “internal” (subjective) volatility over shorter horizons than long ones.
problems.source_evidence: “The quantum walk model may also help to explain the empirically noted property that the implied volatility includes a time-dependent term that varies inversely with the square root of the time to expiry ...” and “the incompatibility between internal (subjective) and measured (objective) growth rates ... may therefore manifest itself as an adjustment to option prices (not modeled).”
problems.explanation: The memo omits the explicit limitation that the time-dependent/internal-volatility effect is not modeled in the option prices themselves. The paper flags this as an unmodeled adjustment, which is a substantive caveat.

problems.memo_sentence: The author acknowledges that the quantum-walk model tends to assign unrealistically low probability to the purchase of far out–of–the–money options, highlighting a behavioral/empirical mismatch that the current formulation does not fully resolve.
problems.source_evidence: “One unrealistic feature of the quantum model is that it tends to assign very low probability to the purchase of options that are far out-of-the-money. According to Bergsma et al. (2019), ‘informed traders’ ... often prefer to use options that are out-of-the-money because they offer higher leverage. In contrast, less sophisticated traders may be attracted by the opportunity to make lottery-style bets on big price changes. Such effects could be accounted for in a more complicated model by including a population of purchasers who use the classical model, rather than the quantum model; or by modifying the purchase propensity function to include behavioral effects.”
problems.explanation: The memo captures the low-probability limitation but omits the paper’s explanation and proposed remedies: informed traders may prefer OTM options, and the author suggests adding classical purchasers or behavioral effects. That is a meaningful nearby caveat.

problems.memo_sentence: The paper addresses European option pricing by proposing a quantum-walk-based alternative to the classical random walk/binomial framework, modeling the evolution of investors’ beliefs about future log-prices rather than observed stock-price paths.
problems.source_evidence: The paper’s later sections state: “The quantum walk model may also help to explain the empirically noted property that the implied volatility includes a time-dependent term that varies inversely with the square root of the time to expiry ...” and “The resulting surface resembles the implied volatility surfaces obtained from empirical analysis of option price data ...” and “The resulting model can be viewed as a market compromise between the quantum and classical models ...”
problems.explanation: The memo is heavily weighted toward the abstract/introduction framing and underrepresents the paper’s later results/discussion about implied-volatility surfaces, transaction volume, and the market-compromise construction. This is not a factual error, but it is a noticeable section imbalance.
